docs.compound: Das Present Perfect wird mit 'have/has' + Partizip Perfekt gebildet (I have worked, she has worked). Bei regelmäßigen Verben ist das Partizip identisch mit der Präteritumform auf -ed (worked, loved, studied).

groups.name: Regelmäßige Verben (Standardgruppe, z. B. auf Konsonant)
groups.note: Man nimmt den Infinitiv ohne 'to' als Stamm (work); dieser Stamm bleibt in allen Formen unverändert.

groups.name: Verben auf -e
groups.note: Der Stamm ist der Infinitiv ohne 'to' (love); in der Vergangenheit wird nur -d angehängt, weil das -e schon da ist.

groups.name: Verben auf Konsonant + -y
groups.note: Bei Konsonant + y wird das y vor -s und -ed zu i: study → studies, studied (bei Vokal + y wie 'play' bleibt das y: plays, played).

patterns.explain: Verben auf -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -z und -o erhalten in der 3. Person Singular die Endung -es statt -s. Das erleichtert die Aussprache.
patterns.title: Besonderheit bei he/she/it: -es

patterns.explain: Viele unregelmäßige Verben haben für Präteritum und Partizip dieselbe Form. Diese Formen muss man auswendig lernen.
patterns.title: Gleiche Form in Präteritum und Partizip

patterns.explain: Manche Verben haben im Infinitiv, Präteritum und Partizip jeweils eine eigene Form, ähnlich wie deutsche starke Verben (singen – sang – gesungen).
patterns.title: Drei verschiedene Formen

patterns.explain: Einige Verben bleiben in allen drei Grundformen gleich. Die Zeit erkennt man nur am Kontext.
patterns.title: Unveränderte Verben

patterns.explain: Bei manchen Verben ändert sich der Stammvokal in der Vergangenheit, und das Partizip kann gleich bleiben oder sich ändern.
patterns.title: Vokalwechsel

tips: Im Präsens gibt es nur eine Besonderheit: he/she/it bekommt ein -s (oder -es/-ies). Alle anderen Personen haben die Grundform.
Das Präteritum ist für alle Personen gleich, es gibt keine Personalendungen. Nur 'to be' hat zwei Formen: was und were.
Lerne unregelmäßige Verben immer in drei Formen (Infinitiv – Präteritum – Partizip), z. B. speak – spoke – spoken, und nutze deutsche Ähnlichkeiten wie singen – sang – gesungen als Gedächtnisstütze.

docs.compound: El Present perfect se forma con el auxiliar have/has + participio pasado (have worked, has lived). En los verbos regulares el participio termina igual que el pasado simple: -ed, -d o -ied.

groups.name: Verbos regulares terminados en consonante (la mayoría)
groups.note: Se usa el infinitivo sin 'to' como raíz; no cambia, solo se añade -s en la 3.ª persona del singular en presente y -ed en pasado.

groups.name: Verbos terminados en -e
groups.note: La raíz es el infinitivo sin 'to'; en pasado solo se añade -d porque ya termina en -e.

groups.name: Verbos terminados en consonante + -y
groups.note: La -y cambia a -i antes de -es y -ed; con vocal + y (play) no cambia: plays, played.

patterns.explain: En muchos verbos irregulares el pasado simple y el participio tienen la misma forma. Hay que aprenderlos de memoria.
patterns.title: Participio y pasado iguales

patterns.explain: El infinitivo, el pasado y el participio son diferentes entre sí; suele cambiar la vocal de la raíz.
patterns.title: Cambio de vocal (tres formas distintas)

patterns.explain: Algunos verbos forman el participio con la terminación -n o -en, a menudo con cambio de vocal.
patterns.title: Participio con -n / -en

patterns.explain: Algunos verbos tienen la misma forma en infinitivo, pasado y participio.
patterns.title: Verbos que no cambian

tips: En presente solo la 3.ª persona del singular (he/she/it) lleva terminación: -s, -es o -ies. Es el error más frecuente de los hispanohablantes.
A diferencia del español, el inglés necesita siempre el pronombre sujeto (I work, no 'work').
Aprende los verbos irregulares en tres columnas: infinitivo – pasado – participio, y repásalos en voz alta con frecuencia.

rules: Chaque mot de plus d'une syllabe a une syllabe accentuée, et les autres sont faibles et courtes.
Le « th » se prononce avec la langue entre les dents : /θ/ dans « think », /ð/ dans « this ».
Le « h » est aspiré au début de la plupart des mots : on expire dans « hello », « house ».
Les voyelles non accentuées deviennent souvent un son neutre /ə/ : « banana », « about ».
topics.summary: L'anglais s'écrit souvent autrement qu'il ne se prononce. L'accent tonique (la syllabe prononcée plus fort) est essentiel pour être compris.
topics.tip: Les Français accentuent la dernière syllabe. En anglais, ce n'est presque jamais le cas : dites « HO-tel », « CHOC-o-late », « PHO-to-graph ».
topics.title: Prononciation et accent tonique

rules: Utilisez « a » devant un son de consonne et « an » devant un son de voyelle (selon le son, pas la lettre).
« The » remplace « le, la, les » et ne change jamais.
On n'utilise pas d'article devant les noms pluriels ou indénombrables pris en général.
Les objets n'ont pas de genre : on dit « it » pour une chose.
topics.summary: L'anglais a un article indéfini (a/an) et un seul article défini (the). Il n'y a pas de genre grammatical pour les noms.
topics.tip: Piège : « I like coffee », sans « the », quand on parle en général. Et on dit « an hour » car le h est muet.
topics.title: Articles : a, an, the

examples.de: Il y a beaucoup de gens.
examples.x: There are a lot of people.

rules: En général, on ajoute -s : « book → books ».
Après -s, -x, -ch, -sh, on ajoute -es : « bus → buses ».
Consonne + y devient -ies : « city → cities ».
Quelques pluriels irréguliers sont à connaître : man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people.
topics.summary: Le pluriel se forme presque toujours avec un -s, mais quelques noms courants sont irréguliers.
topics.tip: Le -s final se prononce /s/, /z/ ou /ɪz/. Attention : « news », « information » et « luggage » sont indénombrables, donc sans -s : « some information ».
topics.title: Pluriel des noms

rules: L'adjectif précède le nom : « a red car ».
Il ne prend jamais de -s au pluriel : « red cars ».
Après « be », il se place après le verbe : « The car is red ».
Pour comparer, on ajoute -er aux mots courts et « more » aux mots longs : « cheaper », « more expensive ».
topics.summary: En anglais, l'adjectif se place avant le nom et ne s'accorde jamais en genre ni en nombre.
topics.tip: Erreur typique : « a car red » ou « reds cars ». Placez l'adjectif devant et ne lui ajoutez jamais de -s.
topics.title: Adjectifs : place et invariabilité

rules: Pronoms sujets : I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
Pronoms compléments : me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
Le sujet est toujours obligatoire : « It is cold », jamais « Is cold ».
On exprime la politesse avec « Could you… ? », « Would you like… ? » et « please ».
topics.summary: L'anglais n'a qu'un seul « you » pour tu et vous. La politesse passe par le ton et des formules comme « could you » et « please ».
topics.tip: Pas de tu/vous : « you » convient partout. N'oubliez pas le sujet : « It is late », pas « Is late ».
topics.title: Pronoms personnels et politesse

examples.de: Elle prend le train chaque matin.
examples.x: She takes the train every morning.

rules: À he/she/it, on ajoute -s au verbe : « she works ».
Les autres personnes gardent la forme de base : « I work, they work ».
On utilise le présent simple pour les habitudes : « I take the bus every day ».
Pour une action en cours, on utilise be + verbe en -ing : « I am working ».
topics.summary: Le présent simple décrit les habitudes et les faits. Le verbe ne change qu'à la 3e personne du singulier.
topics.tip: Le -s de la 3e personne est l'oubli le plus courant : « he work » est faux, dites « he works ». Le français ne distingue pas « I eat » et « I am eating », l'anglais si.
topics.title: Présent : be, have et présent simple

examples.x: I am going to the station.

rules: Be : I am, you are, he/she/it is, we are, they are.
Have : have, mais « has » à he/she/it.
Do : do, mais « does » à he/she/it, et il sert d'auxiliaire pour les questions et négations.
Go, get, make, take et want sont très utiles au quotidien.
topics.summary: Quelques verbes très fréquents ont des formes particulières qu'il faut apprendre par cœur.
topics.tip: En français on dit « j'ai 30 ans » et « j'ai faim », mais en anglais on utilise « be » : « I am 30 », « I am hungry ».
topics.title: Verbes irréguliers essentiels

examples.de: Nous sommes allés à Londres l'an dernier.
examples.x: We went to London last year.
Have you ever tried this dish?

rules: Le prétérit des verbes réguliers prend -ed : « visited ». Les irréguliers sont à apprendre : go → went, see → saw.
Avec un moment précis du passé (yesterday, last week), on utilise le prétérit.
Le present perfect se forme avec have/has + participe passé : « I have seen ».
Il s'emploie pour l'expérience ou un résultat présent, avec « ever », « never », « already », « yet ».
topics.summary: Le prétérit raconte un fait terminé à un moment précis. Le present perfect relie le passé au présent.
topics.tip: Le passé composé français correspond souvent au prétérit anglais. Ne dites pas « I have seen him yesterday » : avec « yesterday », dites « I saw him yesterday ».
topics.title: Passé : prétérit et present perfect

examples.de: Nous allons visiter Rome cet été.
examples.x: We are going to visit Rome this summer.
I will call you when I arrive.

rules: « Will » + verbe de base exprime une décision spontanée, une promesse ou une prévision.
« Be going to » + verbe exprime un projet déjà décidé ou une prévision basée sur un indice.
Le présent continu peut exprimer un rendez-vous prévu : « I am meeting Tom tomorrow ».
Après « when », « if » et « as soon as », on utilise le présent, pas « will ».
topics.summary: L'anglais n'a pas de terminaison de futur. On utilise « will » ou « be going to » selon l'intention.
topics.tip: Erreur fréquente : « when I will arrive ». Après « when » et « if », on met le présent : « when I arrive ».
topics.title: Futur : will et going to

examples.de: Je ne parle pas anglais couramment.

rules: Au présent : « don't » (« doesn't » à he/she/it) + verbe de base.
Au passé : « didn't » + verbe de base, qui ne prend alors ni -ed ni forme irrégulière.
Avec « be » et les modaux (can, will), on ajoute simplement « not » : « isn't », « can't », « won't ».
Une seule négation par phrase : « I don't want anything », pas « nothing » en plus.
topics.summary: Pour nier, on utilise l'auxiliaire « do » + not, sauf avec « be » et les modaux.
topics.tip: Après « doesn't » ou « didn't », le verbe reste à la base : « she doesn't works » et « I didn't went » sont faux.
topics.title: Négation

examples.de: À quelle heure part le train ?
examples.x: What time does the train leave?

rules: Au présent : « Do/Does + sujet + verbe ? ». Au passé : « Did + sujet + verbe de base ? ».
Avec « be » et les modaux, on inverse simplement : « Are you ready? », « Can I sit here? ».
Avec un mot interrogatif : mot interrogatif + auxiliaire + sujet + verbe : « Where do you live? ».
Les mots interrogatifs : what, where, when, who, why, how, how much, how many.
topics.summary: En anglais, la question utilise souvent l'auxiliaire « do », et l'ordre des mots reste strict.
topics.tip: Ne calquez pas « est-ce que » : l'anglais n'a pas d'équivalent. N'inversez pas verbe et sujet sans auxiliaire : « Speak you English? » est faux.
topics.title: Questions

examples.de: Nous nous retrouvons lundi devant l'hôtel.
examples.x: We meet on Monday in front of the hotel.

rules: L'ordre normal est sujet + verbe + complément : « I need a taxi ».
Temps : « at » pour l'heure, « on » pour le jour, « in » pour le mois ou l'année : at 5, on Monday, in July.
Lieu : « at » pour un point précis, « in » pour un espace fermé ou une ville, « on » pour une surface.
Le lieu précède généralement le temps : « I work in Lyon on Mondays ».
topics.summary: L'ordre de base est sujet + verbe + complément. Les prépositions de lieu et de temps ne se traduisent pas toujours mot à mot.
topics.tip: Piège : « on Monday » et non « in Monday ». Le français « à/en/dans » correspond à plusieurs prépositions anglaises, donc apprenez-les en expressions toutes faites.
topics.title: Prépositions et ordre des mots

examples.de: Je voudrais une table pour deux.
examples.x: I would like a table for two.

rules: Après un modal, le verbe reste à la base, sans « to » ni -s : « she can swim ».
« Can » exprime la capacité ou la permission, « could » est plus poli.
« Should » donne un conseil, « must » une obligation forte.
« Would like » est la manière polie d'exprimer un souhait : « I would like a coffee ».
topics.summary: Les verbes modaux (can, could, should, must…) expriment la capacité, la permission, le conseil ou l'obligation. Ils sont très utiles en voyage.
topics.tip: Erreur courante : « he cans » ou « I can to go ». Les modaux ne prennent jamais de -s ni de « to » après eux.
topics.title: Verbes modaux et demandes courantes

rules: Das „th“ spricht man mit der Zunge zwischen den Zähnen: stimmlos wie in „think“, stimmhaft wie in „this“.
Das „w“ klingt wie ein kurzes „u“ (we, water), das „v“ wie das deutsche „w“ (very).
Meist wird nur eine Silbe im Wort stark betont (z. B. „TAble“, „hoTEL“).
Das „r“ wird weich und ohne Zungenspitzen-Rollen gebildet.
topics.summary: Englisch wird oft anders gesprochen, als es geschrieben wird. Wichtig sind die Wortbetonung und einige Laute, die es im Deutschen nicht gibt.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: „v“ und „w“ vertauschen. „Very“ beginnt mit dem Laut des deutschen „w“, „we“ mit einem „u“-Laut.
topics.title: Aussprache & Betonung

rules: „The“ steht für der, die und das, im Singular wie im Plural.
„A“ steht vor Konsonantenlauten, „an“ vor Vokallauten (a book, an apple).
Im Plural und bei unzählbaren Dingen entfällt der unbestimmte Artikel (books, water).
Dinge haben kein Geschlecht: Sie heißen „it“, nicht „er/sie“.
topics.summary: Englisch kennt keinen grammatischen Artikel-Unterschied nach Geschlecht: Es gibt nur „the“ (bestimmt) und „a/an“ (unbestimmt).
topics.tip: Merke: Es zählt der Laut, nicht der Buchstabe: „an hour“ (h stumm), aber „a university“ (Laut „ju“).
topics.title: Artikel

rules: Regelmäßig hängt man -s an (car → cars), nach s, x, ch, sh -es (bus → buses).
Konsonant + y wird zu -ies (city → cities).
Unregelmäßig sind u. a. man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people.
Unzählbare Wörter wie „water“, „information“, „luggage“ haben keinen Plural.
topics.summary: Die meisten Substantive bilden den Plural einfach mit -s. Einige wichtige Wörter sind unregelmäßig.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: „informations“ oder „luggages“. Diese Wörter bleiben immer im Singular.
topics.title: Plural

rules: Das Adjektiv steht vor dem Substantiv: a big house.
Es hat keine Endungen und passt sich weder an Geschlecht noch an Zahl an.
Steigerung: kurze Adjektive mit -er/-est (small, smaller), lange mit more/most (expensive, more expensive).
Nach „to be“ steht das Adjektiv ohne Artikel: The room is small.
topics.summary: Adjektive (Eigenschaftswörter) stehen vor dem Substantiv und verändern sich nie.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: Endungen wie im Deutschen („a bigs house“). Das Adjektiv bleibt immer gleich.
topics.title: Adjektive

rules: Die Formen: I, you, he, she, it, we, you, they.
„You“ gilt für alle Anredeformen, ein Unterschied zwischen Du und Sie existiert nicht.
Höflichkeit entsteht durch Wörter wie please, thank you, could, would.
„I“ wird immer großgeschrieben.
topics.summary: Personalpronomen sind Wörter wie ich, du, er. Englisch hat nur ein „you“ für du, Sie und ihr.
topics.tip: Statt „Gib mir“ lieber „Could I have …?“ sagen. Direkte Befehle klingen schnell unhöflich.
topics.title: Personalpronomen & Höflichkeit

rules: Das Verb bleibt in der Grundform: I work, you work, we work, they work.
Nur bei he/she/it kommt ein -s dazu: she works.
Für Dinge, die gerade passieren, nutzt man das Present Continuous: am/is/are + Verb-ing.
Wörter wie always, often, never stehen meist vor dem Verb.
topics.summary: Das Simple Present beschreibt Gewohnheiten, Fakten und Fahrpläne. Die Formen sind sehr einfach.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: „I am eating“ und „I eat“ gleichsetzen. Für Jetzt-Handlungen braucht man -ing.
topics.title: Präsens (Simple Present)

rules: „To be“: I am, you are, he/she/it is, we are, they are.
„To have“: I have, aber he/she/it has.
„To do“: he/she/it does; „to go“: he/she/it goes.
Modalverben (can, must, should) bekommen nie ein -s und stehen mit dem Infinitiv ohne „to“.
topics.summary: Einige sehr häufige Verben folgen eigenen Regeln. Diese solltest du zuerst lernen.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: „He can swims“. Nach can steht immer die Grundform.
topics.title: Wichtige unregelmäßige Verben

rules: Regelmäßige Verben bekommen -ed (visit → visited).
Unregelmäßige haben eigene Formen: go → went, see → saw, buy → bought, have → had.
Die Form ist für alle Personen gleich (I went, she went).
Für Verneinung und Fragen nutzt man „did“ plus Grundform.
topics.summary: Das Simple Past beschreibt abgeschlossene Ereignisse in der Vergangenheit. Es wird im Alltag viel verwendet.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: Perfekt wörtlich übersetzen („I have gone yesterday“). Mit „yesterday“ braucht man das Simple Past.
topics.title: Vergangenheit (Simple Past)

examples.de: Ich war noch nie in London.
examples.x: I have never been to London.

examples.de: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier.
examples.x: I have lived here for three years.

rules: Bildung: have/has + Partizip (I have seen, she has eaten).
Man nutzt es für Erfahrungen (ever, never) und Ergebnisse, die jetzt noch wichtig sind.
Mit „for“ (Dauer) und „since“ (Zeitpunkt) beschreibt es etwas, das bis jetzt andauert.
Bei einer genauen Zeitangabe in der Vergangenheit nimmt man das Simple Past.
topics.summary: Das Present Perfect verbindet Vergangenheit und Gegenwart, etwa bei Erfahrungen oder Ergebnissen. Es wird mit have/has plus Partizip gebildet.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: „I live here since three years“. Richtig ist das Present Perfect mit „for“.
topics.title: Present Perfect

examples.de: Wir werden nächste Woche nach Spanien fliegen.
examples.x: We are going to fly to Spain next week.

examples.de: Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.x: If it rains, we will stay at home.

rules: „Will“ + Grundform nutzt man für spontane Entscheidungen und Versprechen.
„Going to“ + Grundform nutzt man für Pläne und sichere Vorhersagen.
Für feste Termine reicht oft das Present Continuous (I am meeting him tomorrow).
Nach „if“ und „when“ steht kein will, sondern das Präsens.
topics.summary: Für die Zukunft gibt es mehrere Formen, die je nach Absicht gewählt werden. Die wichtigsten sind will und going to.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: „If it will rain“. Im if-Satz steht Präsens, im Hauptsatz will.
topics.title: Zukunft

rules: Mit „to be“ und Modalverben: Verb + not (is not/isn’t, cannot/can’t).
Bei anderen Verben nutzt man do/does/did + not + Grundform.
Im Präsens bei he/she/it heißt es „doesn’t“, und das Verb verliert sein -s.
Es gibt keine doppelte Verneinung: I don’t have any money oder I have no money.
topics.summary: Verneinung bildet man im Englischen meist mit einem Hilfsverb plus „not“. Die doppelte Verneinung ist nicht erlaubt.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: „He doesn’t likes“. Nach doesn’t steht immer die Grundform ohne -s.
topics.title: Verneinung

examples.de: Wir treffen uns am Montag um 8 Uhr.

rules: Die Grundreihenfolge ist fest: Subjekt, Verb, Objekt (I like coffee).
Ja/Nein-Fragen: Do/Does/Did + Subjekt + Grundform (Do you speak German?).
Fragewort + Hilfsverb + Subjekt: Where do you live?
Zeit und Ort: „at“ für Uhrzeiten, „on“ für Tage, „in“ für Monate und Orte (at 5, on Monday, in May).
topics.summary: Der englische Satz folgt meist der Reihenfolge Subjekt – Verb – Objekt. Fragen werden meist mit do/does/did gebildet, und Präpositionen (Verhältniswörter wie in, at, on) sind wichtig.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: Die deutsche Wortstellung übernehmen („Today I go to work“ ist okay, aber „Yesterday went I“ nicht). Das Verb steht nach dem Subjekt.
topics.title: Fragen & Satzbau

items.expl: Soft lye pretzel sliced open and spread with butter. Often served as a snack or starter with beer.
items.name: Brezel mit Butter

items.expl: Potato salad, either with a warm vinegar-broth dressing (southern style) or creamy mayonnaise (northern style). Often includes onions and pickles.
items.name: Kartoffelsalat

items.expl: Pan-fried sliced boiled potatoes with onions, often with bacon. Crispy and savory.
items.name: Bratkartoffeln

items.expl: Braised red cabbage cooked with apple, vinegar and spices like cloves. Sweet-sour, served with roasts.
items.name: Rotkohl

items.expl: Fermented shredded white cabbage, cooked until tender, sometimes with juniper and bacon. Tangy and common with sausages and pork.
items.name: Sauerkraut

items.expl: Soft egg noodles from Swabia, pressed or scraped into boiling water. Served plain or with butter.
items.name: Spätzle

items.expl: Large bread dumplings made from stale rolls, milk, eggs and parsley. Served with gravy and roasts.
items.name: Semmelknödel

items.expl: Simple peeled potatoes boiled in salted water. A standard side for meat and fish dishes.
items.name: Salzkartoffeln

items.expl: Thinly sliced cucumber in a dressing of vinegar, oil and dill, or sometimes with sour cream. Fresh and tangy.
items.name: Gurkensalat

items.expl: A thin veal cutlet coated in breadcrumbs and pan-fried until golden. Usually served with a lemon wedge and potato salad or fries.
items.name: Wiener Schnitzel

items.expl: A breaded and fried pork cutlet, the everyday and cheaper version of the classic schnitzel. Often served with fries, potato salad or mushroom sauce.
items.name: Schweineschnitzel

items.expl: A pork or veal cutlet, breaded or plain, served in a creamy brown mushroom sauce. Typically comes with fries, noodles or spätzle.
items.name: Jägerschnitzel

items.expl: A sliced, grilled or fried pork sausage covered in warm curry-spiced ketchup sauce and dusted with curry powder. Sold at street stands with fries or a bread roll.
items.name: Currywurst

items.expl: A grilled pork sausage served in a crusty bread roll with mustard. A classic street food at markets, fairs and stadiums.
items.name: Bratwurst mit Brötchen

items.expl: Small, thin grilled pork sausages seasoned with marjoram from Nuremberg. Usually served in sets of six or more with sauerkraut or potato salad.
items.name: Nürnberger Rostbratwürstchen

items.expl: Roast pork with a crispy crackling crust, slow-cooked in the oven with dark beer or stock. Served with gravy, dumplings and cabbage, especially in Bavaria.
items.name: Schweinebraten

items.expl: A large roasted pork knuckle with crunchy skin and tender meat. Typically served with sauerkraut and dumplings, often to share.
items.name: Schweinshaxe

items.expl: Cured and boiled pork knuckle, very tender and salty, popular in Berlin and northern Germany. Served with sauerkraut and mashed peas.
items.name: Eisbein

items.expl: Beef marinated for days in vinegar, wine and spices, then braised and served in a sweet-sour gravy. Traditionally served with red cabbage and dumplings.
items.name: Sauerbraten

items.expl: Thin slices of beef rolled around bacon, onion, mustard and pickle, then braised in gravy. Served with red cabbage and potatoes or dumplings.
items.name: Rinderroulade

items.expl: Beef rolls filled with bacon, onion, mustard and pickle, braised until tender in a rich brown sauce. A traditional Sunday meal.
items.name: Rouladen

items.expl: Meatballs of minced veal or pork in a creamy white sauce with capers. Usually served with boiled potatoes and sometimes beetroot.
items.name: Königsberger Klopse

items.expl: A pan-fried flat meatball of minced meat, bread roll, egg and onion. Eaten hot with potato salad or cold in a bread roll with mustard.
items.name: Frikadelle

items.expl: German meatloaf made of minced meat, egg, onion and bread, baked in the oven. Served in slices with gravy and mashed potatoes.
items.name: Hackbraten

items.expl: A baked loaf of finely minced pork and beef, similar to a thick bologna, with no liver and no cheese. Eaten hot in slices, often in a roll as a Leberkässemmel.
items.name: Leberkäse

items.expl: Lightly cured and smoked pork loin, served hot in thick slices. Comes with sauerkraut and mashed potatoes.
items.name: Kasseler mit Sauerkraut

items.expl: A Rhineland dish of mashed potatoes and stewed apples, usually topped with fried black pudding and onions. The name means heaven and earth.
items.name: Himmel und Erde

items.expl: A northern German sailors' dish of mashed corned beef, potato and beetroot, topped with a fried egg and served with pickled herring and gherkin.
items.name: Labskaus

items.expl: A bread roll filled with fish such as pickled herring, smoked mackerel or fried fish, with onions and remoulade. A classic snack along the northern coast.
items.name: Fischbrötchen

items.expl: Scrambled eggs served with small North Sea shrimp, often on dark bread. A typical dish in northern coastal restaurants.
items.name: Rührei mit Krabben

items.expl: Soft egg noodles layered with melted cheese and topped with crispy fried onions. A hearty Swabian and Allgäu comfort dish, often with a green salad.
items.name: Käsespätzle

items.expl: Swabian large pasta pockets filled with minced meat, spinach, onion and bread. Served in broth, or sliced and pan-fried with egg.
items.name: Maultaschen

items.expl: Crispy fried pancakes of grated raw potato and onion. Served with apple sauce, or savory with sour cream or smoked salmon.
items.name: Kartoffelpuffer

items.expl: Boiled jacket potatoes served with fresh herb quark, a creamy soft fresh cheese. Often accompanied by linseed oil and a side salad.
items.name: Pellkartoffeln mit Quark

items.expl: Fried herring fillets pickled in a sweet-sour vinegar marinade with onions. Served cold, often with bread or boiled potatoes.
items.name: Bratheringe

items.expl: Pickled herring fillets rolled around a piece of pickle and onion, held with a toothpick. Eaten cold as a snack or with bread.
items.name: Rollmops

items.expl: Whole trout dredged in flour and pan-fried in butter, finished with lemon and parsley. Usually served with boiled potatoes.
items.name: Forelle Müllerin

items.expl: Fresh trout gently poached in a vinegar broth, which turns the skin bluish. Served with melted butter, potatoes and horseradish.
items.name: Forelle blau

items.expl: Pan-fried plaice with crispy bacon and onions, a Hamburg classic. Typically served with potatoes or potato salad.
items.name: Gebratene Scholle Finkenwerder Art

items.expl: Thinly sliced smoked salmon. Served on bread, with scrambled eggs, or with horseradish cream.
items.name: Räucherlachs

items.expl: Breaded and deep-fried white fish fillet, often pollock or cod. Served with potato salad and a lemon wedge.
items.name: Backfisch mit Kartoffelsalat

items.expl: Whole mackerel or whitefish grilled on a stick over embers, a Bavarian beer garden favorite. Eaten by hand with a bread roll.
items.name: Steckerlfisch

items.expl: Pike-perch fillet pan-fried and served in a creamy white wine sauce made with Riesling. Common in wine regions, often with potatoes or vegetables.
items.name: Zander auf Rieslingsoße

items.expl: Bread roll topped with small North Sea shrimp, often with lettuce and a light sauce. Popular at coastal fish stands.
items.name: Krabbenbrötchen

items.expl: Raw herring fillet pickled in vinegar with onions and mustard seeds. Eaten cold with bread or potatoes.
items.name: Bismarckhering

items.expl: Breaded fish fingers made from pollock, baked or fried. Served with mashed potatoes and often spinach or peas, a nostalgic comfort food.
items.name: Fischstäbchen mit Kartoffelpüree

items.expl: Sliced spit-roasted meat, usually veal or chicken, stuffed into flatbread with salad, onions and sauces. Germany's favorite fast food.
items.name: Döner Kebab

items.expl: Sliced fried pork sausage in curry-spiced ketchup sauce, served with a side of fries.
items.name: Currywurst-Pommes

items.expl: French fries topped with ketchup (red) and mayonnaise (white). A classic snack-stand order.
items.name: Pommes rot-weiß

items.expl: Crispy fried grated-potato pancakes from the Rhineland, served with applesauce or sometimes smoked salmon. Common at markets and fairs.
items.name: Reibekuchen

items.expl: Soft pretzel with a dark, salty crust, sold plain in bakeries. Often also available sliced and spread with butter or topped with cheese.
items.name: Laugenbrezel

items.expl: Fluffy yeast doughnut filled with jam and dusted with sugar. Sold in bakeries, especially at carnival time.
items.name: Krapfen

items.expl: Berlin's name for the jam-filled yeast doughnut, usually with plum or strawberry jam and a sugar coating.
items.name: Berliner Pfannkuchen

items.expl: Almonds roasted in caramelized sugar and cinnamon. Sold warm in paper cones at Christmas markets and fairs.
items.name: Gebrannte Mandeln

items.expl: Grilled pork neck steak served in a bread roll, often with onions and mustard. Typical at fairs and football stadiums.
items.name: Steak im Brötchen

items.expl: Plump boiled sausage of pork and beef, served in a roll or with bread and mustard. Found at snack stands and train stations.
items.name: Bockwurst mit Senf

items.expl: Sliced mushrooms fried in a pan with onions and cream or garlic sauce. Sold at Christmas markets and fairs, often with bread.
items.name: Champignonpfanne

items.expl: Whole potato cut into a long spiral, deep-fried on a skewer and seasoned. A popular snack at markets and festivals.
items.name: Kartoffelspirale

items.expl: Thin, flaky pastry rolled around spiced apples, raisins and cinnamon, baked and dusted with powdered sugar. Often served warm with vanilla sauce or ice cream.
items.name: Apfelstrudel

items.expl: Black Forest cake with layers of chocolate sponge, whipped cream and sour cherries, soaked in cherry schnapps (Kirschwasser). Topped with chocolate shavings.
items.name: Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte

items.expl: Yeast cake topped with caramelized almonds and filled with vanilla custard or cream. Found in nearly every German bakery.
items.name: Bienenstich

items.expl: German-style cheesecake made with quark (fresh curd cheese) rather than cream cheese, so it is lighter and slightly tangy. Usually baked on a shortcrust base.
items.name: Käsekuchen

items.expl: A thick red berry compote made from red currants, raspberries and strawberries, served chilled with vanilla sauce or cream. A classic from northern Germany.
items.name: Rote Grütze mit Vanillesoße

items.expl: Large steamed yeast dumpling filled with plum jam, topped with melted butter, poppy seeds and powdered sugar. Often served with vanilla sauce, popular at ski huts and Christmas markets.
items.name: Germknödel

items.expl: Fluffy shredded pancake with raisins, caramelized and dusted with powdered sugar. Typically served with apple sauce or plum compote.
items.name: Kaiserschmarrn

items.expl: Soft gingerbread-like cookie spiced with cinnamon, cloves and ginger, often with nuts and coated in chocolate or sugar glaze. Especially popular around Christmas, with Nuremberg being famous for it.
items.name: Lebkuchen

items.expl: Fluffy steamed yeast dumpling with a caramelized crust on the bottom. Served warm with vanilla sauce.
items.name: Dampfnudel mit Vanillesoße

items.expl: Thin yeast-dough cake topped with halved plums and baked on a sheet, sometimes with streusel. Typical in late summer and autumn, especially in Bavaria.
items.name: Zwetschgendatschi

items.expl: Creamy cake made with sponge and egg liqueur, a sweet, custard-like alcoholic drink. Often layered with whipped cream.
items.name: Eierlikör-Torte

items.expl: Thin, crisp spiced shortcrust biscuits flavored with cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg. Sold in supermarkets mainly in autumn and winter.
items.name: Spekulatius

items.expl: Crusty white bread roll thickly covered with poppy seeds. Eaten at breakfast with butter, jam or cheese.
items.name: Mohnbrötchen

items.expl: Bread roll topped with baked, melted cheese. Eaten warm as a snack or with breakfast.
items.name: Käsebrötchen

items.expl: Sweet yeast pastry rolled in a spiral with raisins and cinnamon, often with a sugar glaze or custard. Common as a breakfast treat.
items.name: Rosinenschnecke

items.expl: Flaky, buttery pastry rolled with cinnamon and sugar, a specialty of Hamburg. Similar to a cinnamon roll but crisper.
items.name: Franzbrötchen

items.expl: Soft, lightly sweet yeast roll with raisins. Usually eaten with butter for breakfast.
items.name: Rosinenbrötchen

items.expl: Dense, hearty wholegrain bread made from rye or wheat, often with seeds. Served sliced with butter, cold cuts or cheese.
items.name: Vollkornbrot

items.expl: Small, deep-fried dough balls made with quark, rolled in sugar. Soft inside and slightly crisp outside.
items.name: Quarkbällchen

items.expl: Pretzel sliced open and spread with a thick layer of butter, sold in bakeries as a quick breakfast or snack.
items.name: Butterbrezel

items.expl: Very popular soft drink made of apple juice mixed with sparkling mineral water. Refreshing and less sweet than pure juice.
items.name: Apfelschorle

items.expl: Light beer mixed with lemonade, usually about half and half. Low in alcohol and popular in summer.
items.name: Radler

items.expl: Cloudy wheat beer with fruity, banana and clove notes, served in a tall glass. Especially typical in Bavaria.
items.name: Weizenbier

items.expl: Light, clear, top-fermented beer from Cologne, served in small, slim 0.2-liter glasses.
items.name: Kölsch

items.expl: Dark copper-colored, malty beer from Düsseldorf with a gentle bitterness.
items.name: Altbier

items.expl: Hot mulled red wine spiced with cinnamon, cloves and orange, sold at Christmas markets in mugs. Grape varieties: no fixed varieties, usually a simple red (or sometimes white) base wine such as Dornfelder, Regent or Merlot blends, spiced and sweetened.
items.name: Glühwein

items.expl: Mix of cola and orange soda, a favorite soft drink across Germany. Also sold under brand names like Mezzo Mix.
items.name: Spezi

items.expl: Riesling white wine mixed with sparkling mineral water, a light spritzer common in wine regions and at wine festivals. Grape varieties: 100% Riesling wine, typically mixed about 1:1 with sparkling water.
items.name: Rieslingschorle

items.expl: Classic drip coffee made by pouring hot water through a paper filter, served black in a cup or pot, with milk and sugar on the side. Medium strength and the standard everyday coffee at home, in bakeries and with cake in the afternoon. Achtung: it is not an 'Americano'; it is brewed, not diluted espresso.
items.name: Filterkaffee

items.expl: A long, black coffee made on a fully automatic machine, with a thin layer of crema on top. It is milder than espresso but stronger in feel than filter coffee, served in a normal cup (about 150-200 ml). Common in restaurants and cafés after a meal. Achtung: it is not an espresso, and it is served black unless you ask for milk.
items.name: Kaffee Crema

items.expl: Strong coffee or a double espresso with a lot of hot milk and a little foam, served in a large bowl-like cup (250-350 ml). Typically a breakfast drink in cafés. Achtung: it is similar to a 'latte' or 'café au lait', but usually has less foam than a US-style latte and is served in a wide cup.
items.name: Milchkaffee

items.expl: A tall glass of warm milk with a shot of espresso poured in, creating layers, topped with milk foam. Mild, creamy, about 250-300 ml, drunk in cafés at any time of day, often with flavored syrup. Achtung: in Italy 'latte' alone gets you just milk, and in the US a 'latte' is a bit different; here you must say 'Latte Macchiato'.
items.name: Latte Macchiato

items.expl: Espresso with steamed milk and a thick layer of milk foam, often sprinkled with cocoa powder, in a small to medium cup (150-200 ml). Drunk in the morning and through the day in cafés. Achtung: in Germany it can be served with whipped cream or cocoa in some places, and it is drunk at any hour, unlike in Italy where it is a morning drink.
items.name: Cappuccino

items.expl: A small, very strong shot of coffee (about 30 ml) with crema, served in a tiny cup, often with a sugar packet. Drunk after dinner or as a quick pick-me-up. Achtung: if you order 'einen Kaffee' you will not get an espresso, so ask for it by name.
items.name: Espresso

items.expl: An espresso 'marked' with a small spoonful of milk foam, served in a small cup. Strong and slightly softened, drunk quickly at the bar or after a meal. Achtung: it is not the same as a 'Latte Macchiato' or the large caramel macchiato you may know from coffee chains.
items.name: Espresso Macchiato

items.expl: A double espresso with finely steamed milk and very little foam, in a small to medium cup (about 160-200 ml). Found in modern specialty cafés, strong and smooth, drunk in the morning or afternoon. Achtung: it comes from Australia/New Zealand and is only offered in trendier cafés, not in traditional bakeries.
items.name: Flat White

items.expl: A long coffee similar to Kaffee Crema, brewed to be a little longer than an espresso, mostly in Southern Germany. Served black in a medium cup, mild to medium strength, often in restaurants after meals. Achtung: in Switzerland and Austria the name can mean slightly different things, and in France 'café crème' is coffee with milk, like a latte.
items.name: Café Crème

items.expl: A North Frisian specialty: hot coffee with a shot of rum and a cap of whipped cream, served in a cup with a saucer so the cream hides the alcohol. Sweet, strong and warming, drunk in the afternoon or evening on the North Sea coast, especially in cold weather. Achtung: it contains alcohol, so it is not an ordinary 'coffee with cream'.
items.name: Pharisäer

items.expl: Cold coffee served in a tall glass with two scoops of vanilla ice cream, topped with whipped cream and sometimes chocolate sauce. It is more of a dessert, sweet and creamy, popular in ice cream parlors and cafés in summer. Achtung: it is not iced coffee as in the US or UK, which is simply chilled coffee without ice cream.
items.name: Eiskaffee

items.expl: Hot filter coffee with Irish whiskey and sugar, topped with lightly whipped cream, served in a glass. Strong and warming, drunk in the evening in bars and restaurants or at Christmas markets. Achtung: it contains whiskey, so do not order it as a normal morning coffee.
items.name: Irish Coffee

items.expl: Pale golden, crisp lager with a pronounced hoppy bitterness, about 4.8% ABV. Germany's most popular style, found everywhere; order a 'kleines Pils' (0.2-0.3 l) or a 'großes Pils' (0.4-0.5 l).
items.name: Pils

items.expl: Pale, soft and malty Bavarian lager with gentle hop bitterness, about 4.7-5% ABV. Typical in Munich beer gardens, served in a 0.5 l glass or a 1 l Maß.
items.name: Helles

items.expl: Golden lager, a bit fuller and maltier and less bitter than Pils, about 5% ABV. Common in Dortmund and western Germany, usually served in 0.3 or 0.5 l glasses.
items.name: Export

items.expl: Dark brown Bavarian lager with roasted, bready and slightly caramel flavors and low bitterness, about 5% ABV. Typically drunk with hearty pork dishes in Bavarian pubs, in 0.5 l glasses.
items.name: Dunkel

items.expl: Almost black lager that tastes of light roast and chocolate yet is smooth and not heavy, about 4.5-5% ABV. Popular in Thuringia and Saxony, served in 0.3 or 0.5 l glasses.
items.name: Schwarzbier

items.expl: Strong, malty lager with a rich, sweetish, toasty character, about 6.5-7% ABV. Often a seasonal beer in autumn and winter; served in small 0.3 l or 0.5 l glasses.
items.name: Bock

items.expl: Very strong, dark and malty lager with notes of caramel and dried fruit, about 7-9% ABV. Famous around Lent as 'Starkbier' in Munich; sip it slowly from a 0.5 l glass.
items.name: Doppelbock

items.expl: Light, cloudy and tart wheat beer with low alcohol, about 3% ABV. In Berlin it is traditionally served with a shot of raspberry (rot) or woodruff (grün) syrup in a wide bowl-shaped glass.
items.name: Berliner Weisse

items.expl: Dark lager brewed with smoked malt, so it tastes of bacon and campfire, about 5% ABV. A specialty of Bamberg, drunk in traditional taverns, usually in 0.5 l glasses or mugs.
items.name: Rauchbier

items.expl: Unfiltered, slightly cloudy lager with a fresh, malty and gently hoppy taste, about 5% ABV. Typical of Franconian beer cellars and beer gardens, often served in a stoneware mug or 0.5 l glass.
items.name: Kellerbier

items.expl: White wine made from 100% Riesling grapes, dry with crisp acidity and notes of citrus and green apple. Grown in regions such as the Pfalz, Rheingau and Mosel; goes well with fish, poultry and light dishes.
items.name: Riesling trocken

items.expl: Light white wine from 100% Riesling, usually off-dry to lightly sweet with peach and apple notes and bright acidity. Typical of the Mosel, low in alcohol, and nice as an aperitif or with spicy food.
items.name: Riesling Kabinett

items.expl: White wine from 100% Grauburgunder (Pinot Gris), usually dry, with a full body and flavors of pear, nuts and a little spice. Popular from Baden and the Pfalz; pairs with veal, poultry and creamy dishes.
items.name: Grauburgunder

items.expl: Dry white wine from 100% Weißburgunder (Pinot Blanc), mild and elegant with apple, pear and light nutty notes. Common in Baden and the Pfalz; a versatile food wine for asparagus, fish and salads.
items.name: Weißburgunder

items.expl: Dry white wine from 100% Silvaner, earthy and herbal with subtle fruit and mild acidity. The classic wine of Franken, usually in a flat 'Bocksbeutel' bottle; goes well with asparagus and regional fish.
items.name: Silvaner

items.expl: Light, mild white wine from 100% Müller-Thurgau (Rivaner), with soft acidity and floral, muscat-like fruitiness. Popular as an easy everyday wine from Franken, Baden and the Mosel; good by the glass in summer.
items.name: Müller-Thurgau

items.expl: Red wine from 100% Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir), light to medium-bodied and usually dry, with cherry and berry flavors. Grown in Baden, Pfalz, Württemberg and the Ahr; pairs with duck, game and mushroom dishes.
items.name: Spätburgunder

items.expl: Deep-colored, fruity red wine from 100% Dornfelder with blackberry and cherry notes and soft tannins. Mostly from the Pfalz and Rheinhessen, served by the glass in wine taverns; good with sausages and grilled meat.
items.name: Dornfelder

items.expl: Light, fruity red wine from Württemberg, mostly Trollinger with some Lemberger added for color and structure. Often drunk in a 0.25 l Viertele glass with Swabian dishes such as Maultaschen.
items.name: Trollinger mit Lemberger

items.expl: Rosé wine made from a single red grape variety, often Spätburgunder, and labeled with that variety. Fresh and fruity with strawberry notes and usually off-dry to dry; popular in summer from Baden and Württemberg.
items.name: Weißherbst

items.expl: German sparkling wine, usually from Riesling, Pinot varieties or a blend, ranging from brut (dry) to mild (sweet). Served chilled as an aperitif or for celebrations; 'Winzersekt' comes from a single estate and is often higher quality.
items.name: Sekt

items.expl: Partly fermented young wine from white grapes (often Müller-Thurgau or Riesling), cloudy, sweet and slightly fizzy, around 4-10% ABV and rising as it ferments. Sold in early autumn and traditionally enjoyed with Zwiebelkuchen (onion tart).
items.name: Federweißer

docs.compound: The Perfekt (present perfect) is formed with a conjugated form of haben or sein plus the past participle at the end of the clause: Ich habe gemacht. Regular participles are ge- + stem + -t (gemacht, gearbeitet, gereist); verbs of motion or change of state usually take sein (Ich bin gereist).

groups.name: Regular verbs on -en (standard)
groups.note: Drop -en from the infinitive to get the stem (mach-), then add the personal endings.

groups.name: Stems ending in -t, -d, -n/-m after a consonant (extra -e-)
groups.note: Take the stem (arbeit-) and insert an -e- before -st, -t and -te endings so the word stays pronounceable.

groups.name: Stems ending in -s, -ß, -z, -x (du-form -t)
groups.note: The stem (reis-) already ends in an s-sound, so the du-ending is just -t instead of -st.

patterns.explain: Many strong verbs change the stem vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms of the present. The other forms stay regular.
patterns.title: Vowel change e → i / e → ie (du and er/sie/es)

patterns.explain: Some verbs with stem vowel a add an umlaut in the du and er/sie/es forms of the present.
patterns.title: Vowel change a → ä (du and er/sie/es)

patterns.explain: Strong verbs form the participle with ge- + stem + -en, and the stem vowel often changes.
patterns.title: Strong participles ending in -en

patterns.explain: Mixed verbs change the stem vowel in the past but keep the regular -t endings, so the participle is ge- + changed stem + -t.
patterns.title: Mixed verbs (vowel change + -t ending)

patterns.explain: Modal verbs change the stem vowel in the singular and have no ending in the ich and er/sie/es forms.
patterns.title: Modal verbs (ich/er forms identical, no ending)

tips: The wir and sie/Sie forms are always identical to the infinitive (except sein: wir sind), so learn the infinitive well.
Vowel changes (e → i/ie, a → ä) happen only in du and er/sie/es, never in ich, wir, ihr or sie/Sie.
Modal verbs and wissen have no ending in the ich and er/sie/es forms (ich kann, er kann; ich weiß, er weiß).

docs.compound: Le present perfect se forme avec l'auxiliaire have (has à la 3e personne du singulier) + le participe passé. Pour les verbes réguliers, le participe passé est identique au prétérit et se termine en -ed (I have worked, she has worked).

groups.name: Verbes réguliers (une seule conjugaison, sans groupes par terminaison)
groups.note: On part de l'infinitif sans « to » (work) : ce radical sert de base à toutes les formes, et on ajoute seulement -s à la 3e personne du singulier au présent.

groups.name: Verbes en -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o (variante orthographique)
groups.note: Ces verbes prennent -es (et non -s) à la 3e personne du singulier au présent ; le prétérit reste en -ed.

groups.name: Verbes en consonne + -y (variante orthographique)
groups.note: Le -y devient -ies à la 3e personne du singulier au présent et -ied au prétérit.

patterns.explain: Chez beaucoup de verbes irréguliers, le prétérit et le participe passé ont la même forme, qu'il faut apprendre par cœur.
patterns.title: Prétérit et participe identiques (forme unique)

patterns.explain: La voyelle du radical change au prétérit, et le participe passé prend souvent une terminaison en -n.
patterns.title: Changement de voyelle : trois formes différentes

examples.forms: read / read (prononcé /red/ au prétérit et au participe)

patterns.explain: Certains verbes gardent la même forme à l'infinitif, au prétérit et au participe passé.
patterns.title: Verbes invariables

patterns.explain: Un petit groupe de verbes alterne les voyelles i, a, u entre l'infinitif, le prétérit et le participe passé.
patterns.title: Changement de voyelle I – A – U

tips: Au présent, un seul -s à retenir : he/she/it works. Tous les autres sujets gardent la forme de base.
Le prétérit régulier est toujours en -ed et ne change pas selon la personne ; le futur se forme avec will + infinitif sans « to ».
Apprenez les verbes irréguliers par séries de trois formes (infinitif – prétérit – participe passé), par exemple speak – spoke – spoken.

rules: Say 'ei' like English 'eye' and 'ie' like English 'ee' (Wein = vine, Wien = Vienna).
'w' is pronounced like English 'v', 'v' like 'f', and 'z' like 'ts' (Wasser, Vater, Zeit).
Umlauts change the vowel: ä is like 'e' in 'bed', ö is like 'e' in 'her' with rounded lips, ü is like 'ee' with rounded lips.
'ch' after a, o, u, au is a throaty sound (Bach); after other letters it is a soft hiss (ich); 'sch' is 'sh'.
topics.summary: German is mostly phonetic: once you know the sound rules, you can read almost any word aloud. Stress usually falls on the first syllable of a word.
topics.tip: Don't pronounce 'w' like English 'w'. Say 'Wasser' as 'VAH-ser', not 'WAH-ter'.
topics.title: Pronunciation & Stress

rules: Always capitalize nouns, wherever they appear in the sentence.
Learn each noun together with its article (der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch).
Gender is often not logical, so memorize it with the noun.
Some endings help: -ung, -heit, -keit are feminine; -chen and -lein are neuter; -er for people is often masculine.
topics.summary: Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). All nouns are capitalized.
topics.tip: Never learn 'Tisch', only 'der Tisch'. Guessing the gender from English logic often fails (das Mädchen, 'the girl', is neuter).
topics.title: Nouns, Capitalization & Gender

examples.de: I give the woman the key.
examples.x: Ich gebe der Frau den Schlüssel.

rules: Nominative is the subject: who or what does the action (Der Mann schläft).
Accusative is the direct object: who or what receives the action (Ich sehe den Mann).
Dative is the indirect object: to or for whom (Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch).
Genitive shows possession (das Auto des Mannes), but in speech 'von + dative' is common.
topics.summary: German uses cases to show a noun's job in the sentence. A 'case' is a form of the article (and sometimes the noun) that signals subject, object, and so on.
topics.tip: Only masculine changes in the accusative (der → den). Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same, so start there.
topics.title: The Four Cases

examples.de: I have a brother and a sister.
examples.x: Ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester.

rules: Definite nominative: der / die / das / die (plural).
Accusative changes only masculine: den. Dative: dem / der / dem / den (plural, plus -n on the noun).
Indefinite: ein / eine / ein; accusative masculine is einen; dative is einem / einer / einem.
'Kein' (no, not a) takes the same endings as 'ein'.
topics.summary: Definite (the) and indefinite (a/an) articles change by gender and case. Learning the table once pays off everywhere.
topics.tip: English speakers often forget the dative after verbs like 'helfen' and 'danken'. Memorize them as 'helfen + dative'.
topics.title: Articles & Their Forms

rules: Common endings are -e, -er, -en/-n, -s, or no ending.
Many plurals add an umlaut (der Apfel → die Äpfel; das Buch → die Bücher).
Feminine nouns very often take -n or -en (die Frau → die Frauen).
The plural article is always 'die' in the nominative and accusative.
topics.summary: German forms plurals in several ways, and there is no single rule. Learn the plural together with the noun.
topics.tip: Learn nouns as a trio: der Apfel, die Äpfel. Don't just add '-s' like in English; it is mostly for loanwords (Autos, Handys).
topics.title: Plural Nouns

rules: Use 'du' (plural 'ihr') with friends, family, children and peers; use 'Sie' with strangers, in shops and at work.
'Sie' (formal you) is always capitalized and takes the same verb form as 'sie' (they).
Pronouns change by case: ich/mich/mir, du/dich/dir, er/ihn/ihm, wir/uns/uns.
'Es' is used for neuter nouns and for impersonal phrases (Es regnet).
topics.summary: German has two ways to say 'you': informal 'du' and formal 'Sie'. Choosing the right one matters in daily life.
topics.tip: When unsure, use 'Sie'. Germans will say 'Wir können uns duzen' (we can use 'du') when it's fine to switch.
topics.title: Personal Pronouns & Formal 'You'

examples.x: Wir stehen um sieben Uhr auf.

rules: Endings: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en.
If the stem ends in -t or -d, add an extra -e (du arbeitest, er arbeitet).
Use the present tense for near future too, with a time word (Morgen fahre ich).
Separable verbs split: the prefix goes to the end (aufstehen → Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf).
topics.summary: Regular verbs take the stem (infinitive minus -en) plus personal endings. One present tense covers both 'I work' and 'I am working'.
topics.tip: Don't translate 'I am working' as 'Ich bin arbeiten'. Just say 'Ich arbeite'.
topics.title: Present Tense: Regular Verbs

rules: sein (to be): ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind.
haben (to have): ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie haben.
Some verbs change the stem vowel: e → i/ie (essen → du isst, sehen → du siehst), a → ä (fahren → du fährst).
Modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen, möchten) send the second verb to the end as an infinitive.
topics.summary: The most common verbs, such as sein, haben and werden, are irregular and must be learned by heart. Many others change their vowel in the du and er forms.
topics.tip: Use 'Ich möchte...' (I would like...) for polite requests in restaurants and shops. It is more natural than 'Ich will...', which sounds demanding.
topics.title: Key Irregular Verbs

examples.de: I am staying home because I am sick.
examples.x: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.

examples.de: Tomorrow I am travelling to Munich by train.
examples.x: Morgen fahre ich mit dem Zug nach München.

rules: In main clauses, the verb is in second position (Heute gehe ich einkaufen).
If another element starts the sentence, the subject moves after the verb (Morgen komme ich).
In subordinate clauses (after weil, dass, wenn), the verb goes to the end.
Time comes before manner and place (Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin).
topics.summary: The conjugated verb is the anchor of German sentences. Its position follows firm rules, which differ from English.
topics.tip: After 'weil' English speakers keep the verb in the middle. Remember: the verb goes last (weil ich krank bin).
topics.title: Word Order & Sentence Structure

rules: Predicate adjectives have no ending (Das Haus ist groß).
After 'der/die/das' in the nominative, use -e (der große Hund); in the accusative masculine, use -en (den großen Hund).
After 'ein/eine/ein', the adjective shows the gender: ein großer Hund, eine große Katze, ein großes Haus.
In the dative and plural, the ending is usually -en (mit dem großen Hund).
topics.summary: Adjectives before a noun take endings that depend on gender, case and the article. After the noun with 'sein', they have no ending.
topics.tip: If you are unsure, -e or -en is right in a majority of cases. Native speakers will still understand you if you get an ending wrong.
topics.title: Adjective Endings

rules: Use 'kein' to negate a noun with 'ein' or no article (Ich habe kein Auto).
Use 'nicht' to negate verbs, adjectives, or definite nouns (Ich komme nicht; Das ist nicht gut).
Yes/no questions put the verb first (Sprichst du Deutsch?).
Question words (wer, was, wo, wann, wie, warum) come first, then the verb (Wo wohnst du?).
topics.summary: German uses 'nicht' and 'kein' for negation, and questions are formed by inverting the verb or using question words.
topics.tip: Don't use 'nicht ein' for 'not a'. Say 'kein'. Also, there is no 'do' in German questions: just flip the verb.
topics.title: Negation & Questions

rules: Perfect tense: haben or sein + past participle at the end (Ich habe gegessen).
Use 'sein' with verbs of movement or change of state (Ich bin gefahren, Er ist gekommen).
Regular participles: ge- + stem + -t (gemacht); irregular ones often use ge- + -en (gegangen).
Future: werden + infinitive at the end (Ich werde morgen arbeiten), or simply present + time word.
topics.summary: In speech, Germans use the perfect tense (haben/sein + past participle) for the past. The future uses 'werden' + infinitive, but the present tense often does the job.
topics.tip: For 'sein', 'haben' and modal verbs, Germans prefer the simple past in speech (ich war, ich hatte, ich konnte). Learn these three first.
topics.title: Past Tense & Future

rules: La sílaba tónica (la que se pronuncia con más fuerza) no lleva tilde escrita, así que hay que aprenderla con cada palabra.
La vocal inglesa suele ser más relajada o débil en sílabas átonas (sonido 'schwa', como una 'e' muy suave).
La 'th' se pronuncia con la lengua entre los dientes: /θ/ en 'think' y /ð/ en 'this'.
La 'h' al inicio de palabra se aspira suavemente, como una 'j' muy suave: 'hotel'.
topics.summary: El inglés no se pronuncia como se escribe. Aprender los sonidos clave y dónde cae la sílaba fuerte evita muchos malentendidos.
topics.tip: Error típico: pronunciar 'school' como 'escuela' (eschool). En inglés no se añade una 'e' antes de 's' + consonante: di 'skuul'.
topics.title: Pronunciación y acentuación

rules: Usa 'a' ante sonido de consonante y 'an' ante sonido de vocal: 'a taxi', 'an apple'.
'The' se usa para algo ya conocido o único, y no cambia nunca (ni género ni número).
Con plurales y cosas en general no se usa artículo: 'I like music'.
Cuenta el sonido, no la letra: 'an hour' (la h es muda), 'a university' (suena 'yu').
topics.summary: El inglés tiene un artículo indefinido (a/an) y uno definido (the). No hay género: 'the' sirve para todo.
topics.tip: Error típico: decir 'I like the music' cuando hablas en general, por influencia del español ('me gusta la música'). En inglés se omite 'the'.
topics.title: Artículos: a, an y the

rules: Normalmente se añade -s: 'book → books'; tras -s, -sh, -ch, -x se añade -es: 'bus → buses'.
Consonante + y cambia a -ies: 'city → cities'.
Hay plurales irregulares que conviene memorizar: man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people.
Los incontables (water, money, information, luggage) no tienen plural ni llevan 'a/an'.
topics.summary: Los sustantivos forman el plural de manera sencilla, pero hay irregulares y palabras que no se pueden contar (incontables).
topics.tip: Error típico: decir 'informations' o 'luggages'. Son incontables; usa 'some information' o 'a piece of luggage'.
topics.title: Plurales y sustantivos contables

rules: El sujeto es obligatorio: 'It is cold', no 'Is cold'.
'You' vale para tú, usted, vosotros y ustedes.
Los pronombres son: I, you, he, she, it, we, they; como objeto: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
Para ser cortés usa 'Could you...?', 'Would you like...?' y 'please'.
topics.summary: El inglés siempre necesita sujeto explícito y tiene un solo 'you' para tú y usted. La cortesía se expresa con palabras como 'please' y 'could'.
topics.tip: Error típico: omitir el sujeto ('Is late' en vez de 'It is late'). Recuerda: en inglés una frase casi siempre tiene sujeto.
topics.title: Pronombres personales y cortesía

examples.de: El pasaporte de María está aquí.

rules: El adjetivo va delante del sustantivo: 'a red car'.
El adjetivo no cambia en género ni número: 'big houses', 'a big house'.
Los posesivos son my, your, his, her, its, our, their; 'his/her' depende de quién posee.
Para decir 'de alguien' usa 's: 'Maria's bag'.
topics.summary: Los adjetivos van antes del sustantivo y nunca cambian de forma. Los posesivos concuerdan con el poseedor, no con la cosa poseída.
topics.tip: Error típico: poner el adjetivo detrás ('a car red') o añadir -s al adjetivo ('reds cars'). Piensa: adjetivo delante, siempre invariable.
topics.title: Adjetivos y posesivos

examples.de: El tren sale a las seis.

rules: To be: I am, you are, he/she/it is, we are, they are; sirve para 'ser' y 'estar'.
En presente simple, el verbo no cambia salvo he/she/it, que añade -s: 'she works'.
Con he/she/it, verbos acabados en -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o añaden -es: 'he goes', 'she watches'.
Se usa para rutinas, horarios y hechos: 'The train leaves at six'.
topics.summary: 'To be' (ser/estar) es irregular y esencial. El presente simple sirve para hábitos y hechos, con una -s especial en la tercera persona.
topics.tip: Error típico: olvidar la -s en 'he/she/it' ('she work'). Es la única terminación del presente; no la olvides.
topics.title: Presente simple y el verbo to be

rules: 'Have' (tener) pasa a 'has' con he/she/it: 'she has'.
'Do' pasa a 'does' con he/she/it y es el auxiliar de preguntas y negaciones.
'Go' pasa a 'goes' con he/she/it; 'go to' indica destino.
'Have' también se usa en expresiones: 'have breakfast', 'have a shower'.
topics.summary: Algunos verbos muy frecuentes se comportan de forma especial. Conocerlos facilita el día a día.
topics.tip: Error típico: decir 'He has hunger' por 'tiene hambre'. En inglés se usa 'to be': 'I am hungry/thirsty/cold', y para la edad 'I am 30'.
topics.title: Verbos irregulares esenciales: have, do, go

examples.x: I am waiting for the bus.
She is talking on the phone.

rules: Estructura: am/is/are + verbo-ing: 'I am eating'.
Se usa para lo que pasa ahora o en este periodo: 'I am traveling this week'.
También expresa planes ya organizados: 'We are leaving tomorrow'.
Algunos verbos de estado (know, like, want, need) normalmente no se usan en continuo.
topics.summary: Se usa para acciones que ocurren ahora o planes cercanos. Se forma con 'to be' + verbo con -ing.
topics.tip: Error típico: decir 'I am wanting' o 'I am knowing'. Con verbos de estado se usa el presente simple. Además, el presente simple no sirve para 'ahora mismo': di 'I am eating', no 'I eat' si hablas del momento.
topics.title: Presente continuo

rules: Regulares: verbo + -ed: 'visit → visited'; si acaba en -e solo -d: 'live → lived'.
Irregulares comunes: go → went, have → had, see → saw, buy → bought, eat → ate.
La forma del pasado es la misma para todas las personas: 'I went', 'she went'.
'To be' en pasado: I/he/she/it was, you/we/they were.
topics.summary: Se usa para acciones terminadas en el pasado. Los verbos regulares añaden -ed y hay muchos irregulares muy comunes.
topics.tip: Error típico: confundir con el español, que distingue 'fui/iba'. El inglés usa un solo pasado simple para ambos; el contexto aclara el sentido ('I was tired', 'I went home').
topics.title: Pasado simple

examples.x: I will help you with the suitcase.

examples.de: Voy a visitar Roma en verano.
examples.x: I am going to visit Rome in summer.

rules: 'Will' + verbo base expresa decisiones del momento, promesas y predicciones: 'I will help you'.
'Be going to' + verbo base expresa planes e intenciones ya decididos: 'I am going to visit Rome'.
El verbo tras 'will' nunca cambia: 'she will go', no 'she will goes'.
Con el presente continuo también se expresan planes cercanos: 'We are leaving at noon'.
topics.summary: El inglés no tiene una conjugación de futuro; usa auxiliares. 'Will' y 'going to' tienen usos algo distintos.
topics.tip: Error típico: usar 'will' después de 'when/if' ('If it will rain'). Tras 'if' y 'when' se usa presente: 'If it rains, we will stay'.
topics.title: Futuro: will y going to

examples.de: Ella no fue a la fiesta.
examples.x: She didn't go to the party.

rules: Negación: do/does/did + not + verbo base: 'I don't like', 'she doesn't like', 'he didn't go'.
Pregunta: Do/Does/Did + sujeto + verbo base: 'Do you speak English?'.
Con 'to be' y modales se invierte el orden: 'Are you ready?', 'Can you help?'.
Palabras de pregunta (what, where, when, why, how, who) van al principio: 'Where do you live?'.
topics.summary: En presente y pasado simple, las negaciones y preguntas necesitan el auxiliar 'do/does/did'. Con 'to be' y los modales no hace falta.
topics.tip: Error típico: añadir la -s o el pasado al verbo principal junto con el auxiliar ('Does she works?', 'He didn't went'). El auxiliar ya marca el tiempo; el verbo queda en forma base.
topics.title: Negación y preguntas

examples.de: Nos vemos el lunes a las cinco.
examples.x: We meet on Monday at five.

examples.de: El mapa está sobre la mesa.
examples.x: The map is on the table.
I am waiting for my friend.

rules: Orden básico: sujeto + verbo + objeto + lugar + tiempo: 'I met her at the café yesterday'.
Tiempo: 'at' para horas (at 5), 'on' para días (on Monday), 'in' para meses, años y estaciones (in July).
Lugar: 'at' para punto concreto (at the station), 'in' para espacios cerrados (in the room), 'on' para superficies (on the table).
Algunos verbos llevan preposición fija: 'wait for', 'listen to', 'look at'.
topics.summary: El orden básico es sujeto + verbo + objeto, y es bastante rígido. Las preposiciones de lugar y tiempo son muy frecuentes y no siempre coinciden con el español.
topics.tip: Error típico: traducir preposiciones literalmente ('wait to' o 'listen music'). Aprende los verbos con su preposición: 'wait for', 'listen to'. Recuerda también que el verbo nunca va antes del sujeto en frases afirmativas.
topics.title: Preposiciones y orden de la frase
